new: Over 2,231 years the pointer falls 262° behind, nearly three quarters of a turn. On a round dial that looks the same as 98° ahead, and the Moon's own monthly swing adds the rest.
why: The sentence invites the reader to multiply, and 0.12 by 2,231 is about 268, not the 105 of the next sentence. The first figure also shows the 'slow' pointer ahead of the Moon (+105.3). A reader who notices either stops trusting the page. The story says 'a third of a turn out' as if the pointer had slipped a third of a turn; it has slipped nearly three quarters.
needs: The 262° behind, the 98° ahead and the monthly swing: they are under the fold, in 'The pointers today', in the paragraph that begins 'The Moon is another matter'. 'Nearly three quarters of a turn' is my own division (262 by 360) and wants confirming. Note also that 0.12° a year for 2,231 years is 268°, not 262°; the rate is presumably rounded, so print it as 'about 0.12°' or give one more figure.

old: Even set as well as it could be, the pointer for Mars was at times 35° from the planet, a tenth of the way round the sky.
new: Even set as well as it could be, the pointer for Mars was at times 35° from the planet, a tenth of the way round the sky, and typically about 10° from it; today it would typically be about 12° from it.
why: 'Their typical error has grown by between 11% and 22%' gives a growth without ever giving the size that grew. I went to the picture for the size and found single-day figures that seem to say the opposite. One planet's typical error, then and now, in degrees, would let the percentages mean something.
needs: The typical error of the Mars pointer when new and today. The table under the fold ('The pointers today') has 9.6° and 11.7°. Also what 'typical' is (that table's note says root mean square over 76 years); the story never says, and need not, but the author should be content that 'typically about 10°' is a fair plain reading of it.

old: The pointers for Mercury, Mars and Jupiter would be almost as close to their planets today as when the machine was new.
new: The day in the picture is a kind one: the pointer for Mars is half a degree out only because its two kinds of error happen to cancel. Taken over the years, the pointers for Mercury, Mars and Jupiter would be almost as close to their planets today as when the machine was new.
why: The first figure shows every planet within 7° and Mars within half a degree, and the paragraph after it says Mars was at times 35° out. The story never squares the two, so the picture leaves a rosier impression than the text means to give.
needs: That the day is a lucky one and why. Under the fold, 'The pointers today': 'The day itself is a kind one. Mars is half a degree out because the theory's error and the gears' drift happen to cancel.' 'Taken over the years' stands for the 76 years of that table's note.

old: The ratios are those of a reconstruction published by Freeth and others in 2021, and for the three planets that do well they are that paper's restoration, not numbers read on the machine.
new: The gear ratios I used are those of a reconstruction published by Freeth and others in 2021. For Venus and Saturn, the two that do worse, the numbers are read on the machine's inscriptions; for the three planets that do well they were supplied by that paper.
why: Same 'old' as readable.json planets-3b: use one or the other. 'Not numbers read on the machine' left me asking whether the other two were read on the machine. If they were, that is the most interesting thing in the paragraph (the planets that do well are the ones whose numbers modern scholars supplied) and the story has dropped it.
needs: Whether the ratios for Venus and Saturn are read on the machine. Under the fold, 'What was done': 'for Venus and Saturn the number of years is read on the mechanism's inscriptions, and the other three are their restoration'; the 'In short' box there says the same.

old: one for each month of an eighteen-year cycle of eclipses.
new: one for each month of an eighteen-year cycle of eclipses, a month here being the time from one new moon to the next.
why: A stranger multiplies 18 by 12, gets 216 and wonders at 223.
needs: That the dial's months are months of the Moon. Under the fold, 'The eclipse dial': 'one for each lunar month of an eighteen-year eclipse cycle'.

new: After about 560 years, around AD 355, half of the months marked for the Moon did.
why: 'Half' of what is not said, and this sentence counts years from 205 BC while the next gives years AD. The chart shows 19 of the Moon's 38 at about that point but 16 of the Sun's 28, so 'half' looks true of the Moon's marks and not quite of the Sun's.
needs: (a) Which marks 'half' is said of: the Moon's, the Sun's or all 66 together; the table under the fold has 20 and 16 at 541 years. (b) The year AD that is 560 years after 205 BC; I make it 355 or 356.

old: So the marks go stale from one edge, and a month that has lost its eclipse never gets one back.
new: The months that the dial puts furthest before one of those points lose their eclipses first, and a month that has lost its eclipse never gets one back.
why: Same 'old' as readable.json cause-2: use one or the other. This says what 'from one edge' was trying to say.
needs: Which months fail first. Under the fold, 'The eclipse dial': 'So the dial goes wrong from one edge. The months it puts furthest before a node lose their eclipses first'.

old: Meanwhile real eclipses turn up in months without a mark.
new: Meanwhile real eclipses of the Moon turn up in months without a mark: by 144 years on there were three in a cycle, and from 992 years on the dial missed every one.
why: The heading says the dial would have gone on working, and the count is all one way: of the marked months, how many held an eclipse. A stranger asks the other half at once: how many eclipses came with no mark? The story gives no number.
needs: How many eclipses the dial missed, and when. Under the fold, 'The eclipse dial', the paragraph that begins 'The dial also comes to miss eclipses'; the figures there are for partial or total eclipses of the Moon, which is why 'of the Moon' is added.

old: Of 45 things I expected, 40 proved right.
new: Of 45 things I expected, 40 proved right; the five that did not are listed at the foot of the page.
why: A score with nothing to say what the misses were reads as a boast, and the reader's next question is 'which five?'.
needs: That all five are listed under the fold. I count three and two under 'What I got wrong on the way'. 'Five' is my subtraction.

old: the hours fit four of the sixteen, the starts of 223, 205, 187 and 169 BC, which are one eighteen-year cycle apart. The cycle is about a third of a day longer than a whole number of days, so each of the four fits at a place about a third of the way round the world from the one before.
new: the hours fit four of the sixteen, the starts of 223, 205, 187 and 169 BC. The hour at which an eclipse is seen depends on where one stands, so each start fits the hours only at a certain place, and each of the four at a place about a third of the way round the world from the one before.
why: Same 'old' as readable.json why-2: use one or the other. What a stranger lacks in this paragraph is the reason an hour should 'fit at a place' at all; without it 'puts the dial in the Greek world' arrives from nowhere.
needs: No fact from the study. It states a piece of common knowledge (the clock hour of an eclipse differs from place to place) that the story leaves unsaid, and I may not add it. The author should confirm it is a fair account of how the place comes into the fit ('with the longitude of the place left free', under the fold in 'The hours').

new: by the notes to Freeth's study of the dial,
why: 'Freeth's notes': notes to what? The only Freeth the text has named is 'Freeth and others in 2021', on the planets; the small print inside the second figure has 'Freeth's reconstruction (2014)'. Two papers are going under one name.
needs: That the notes quoted belong to Freeth's 2014 paper on the eclipse dial and not to the 2021 paper. The list of sources under the fold suggests so ('with its supplementary notes').

old: Their reports, and what I got wrong, are at the foot of the page. They share my training and may share my blind spots.
new: Those copies share my training and may share my blind spots. What I got wrong is listed at the foot of the page, with links to their reports.
why: Same 'old' as readable.json trust-1: use one or the other. A reader who opens the fold to find the reports will not find them there; he will find, at the very end, links to them.
needs: Where the reports are. Under the fold, 'How it was checked' says 'Their reports are with the files', and the links are in the last line of 'Sources and files'.

old: Carman and Evans had shown that a scheme like this one drifts and has to be reset, and how the hours fix the year.
new: Carman and Evans had shown that a scheme like the dial's drifts and has to be reset, and how the hours fix the year. Freeth and Jones had found in 2012 that circles on circles leave the pointer for Mars nearly 38° out at times, where I find 35°.
why: Same 'old' as readable.json mine-1: use one or the other. Not a matter of plain wording but of the question whether this section is boastful. It credits the scholars of the eclipse dial and nobody for the planets, so the 35° for Mars reads as this page's own finding.
needs: Whether the 35° had been found before. Under the fold, 'What was already known', last item: Freeth and Jones (2012) found the circle theory for Mars out by 'nearly 38°' at its retrogrades even with a perfect ratio. The same item names a paper of 2021 (Efstathiou and others) that set a simulated mechanism to the present; whether that wants a word beside 'the pointers read off for today' is for the author.

old: I assumed perfect gears, set as well as they could be set.
new: I assumed perfect gears, set as well as they could be set, and a keeper who gave the machine one turn for each year, which is why the Sun's pointer is still right.
why: Two things a stranger asks and the story does not answer: what 'kept turning' means (turned by whom, how often), and what became of the Sun's pointer, which the opening paragraph names and the story never mentions again though the first figure shows it.
needs: How the turning was done and how the Sun's pointer fares. Under the fold, 'What was done': 'I turned the main wheel once for each return of the Sun to the same stars ... A keeper who counted days or months instead would have got other errors'; the table in 'The pointers today' has the Sun 0.18° out over the 76 years to today.
